newsitem.title: INDIA: India rice import plan seen hit by low stocks.
newsitem.headline: India rice import plan seen hit by low stocks.

text.p: India's move to allow free imports of lower grades of rice to stabilise high domestic prices could be a non-starter as big import volumes are unlikely due to high global prices and low supplies, analysts said on Thursday.

"I don't think significant volumes will come in because there are no surplus global stocks (of lower grades of rice)," Ashok Gulati, an economist with the National Council of Applied Economic Research, told Reuters.
India last month allowed the free import of common and coarse grades of rice and rice with 50 percent or more broken content.
The Commerce Ministry said free imports had been permitted after reviewing supply trends and stocks.
Analysts said the main potential suppliers of lower grades of rice to India would be Pakistan, Vietnam and Burma.
"But Vietnam's lower grade varieties are not acceptable in the Indian market and Burma has no stocks," one Bombay-based commodity analyst told Reuters.
"Therefore Pakistan is the only destination which will be able to supply."

Analysts said 60 to 70 percent broken grades of rice were quoted at about 6,500 rupees ($182) per tonne in Indian markets but if the same grade were imported from Pakistan, it would cost more than 7,000 rupees per tonne.
"Imports are not going to be high as the costs associated with imports are relatively high," the analyst said. "But certainly the psychological effect would help stabilise prices to some extent."
India is currently a net exporter of higher grades of non-Basmati and aromatic Basmati rice.

Traders and analysts said export demand for higher grades of Indian rice was dull due to high prices compared with Pakistan and Vietnam. The trend was likely to continue until September when the new crop arrives, they said.
"Our export prices are not in parity with Pakistani and Vietnam prices," said Rashmi Bhimjayani, a leading Bombay foodgrains exporter. "Therefore, we are not able to compete."
Traders said Indian five percent broken non-Basmati rice for export was quoted at $315 per tonne FOB, 10 percent at $300, 15 percent at $260-270 and 25 percent at $250 per tonne.

"We are only competitive in the parboiled rice exports because Pakistan and Vietnam do not produce these varieties," Bhimjayani said. Indian parboiled rice for export was quoted at about $270-$280 per tonne FOB.

Analysts said India's rice exports in the 1996/97 (April-March) year were expected to be about 2.4 million tonnes, out of which two million was non-Basmati and 400,000 tonnes was Basmati variety. Official figures are not yet available.
India exported a record 5.5 million tonnes of rice in 1995/96. Analysts say the fall in exports in 1996/97 was due to a dip in world demand and high Indian prices. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
